title: The Sevapanthis
hook: followers of Bhai Kanhaiya, devoted to quiet service

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirmala learning: teekas and katha, the line on top and the explanation underneath. Your line was explained. When did you stop and ask what someone meant? Day one thousand three hundred seven.

At the end of a big event, the speakers get the applause and the photos. Then the hall empties, and a few people stay behind. They stack the chairs. They wipe the tables. They carry the bins out to the curb in the dark. Nobody films that part. In year one you met Bhai Kanhaiya, the water carrier on the battlefield who, the story says, saw his Guru's face in every wounded man. That was one day of his life. Today is about what came after him: people who made the stay-behind-and-stack-the-chairs part their whole way of life.
screen: `THE SPEAKERS GET THE APPLAUSE.` → `A FEW STAY TO STACK THE CHAIRS.` → `AFTER BHAI KANHAIYA.`

segments.voice: The word is Sevapanthi: one who walks the path of seva, selfless service. Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya's companions and followers formed a community around his way, and that community still exists. Here's what tradition remembers about them. First, service is the center, not a side activity. Sevapanthis are remembered for running places where travelers could rest, drink and eat, and for tending the sick, without asking who anyone was. Second, they lived by their own work. Tradition says they didn't go begging for alms, and that they earned their bread with their hands. Serving others while asking nothing of them was the point. Third, quietness. They're remembered less for great deeds with names attached than for steady work over a long time. So what does the Guru Granth Sahib say about seva? In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak gives a short line. In paraphrase: do seva in this world, and you will find a place to sit in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in this world, among people, in kitchens and on roads. And notice the reward: not applause, a seat. Somewhere to rest, the way a tired traveler finds a seat at a Sevapanthi rest stop. Some Sikhs hear echoes of this in the langar, in the shoe room at the gurdwara where volunteers polish strangers' shoes, in every hand that stacks chairs. The Sevapanthis took that common Sikh practice and made it the name of their path. That's today's line: service first. Not service as a break from real life. Service as the real life, and the rest fitted in around it.
screen: `SEVAPANTHI: THE PATH OF SEVA.` · `REST, WATER AND FOOD FOR ANYONE.` · `BREAD EARNED BY THEIR OWN HANDS.` · `SRI RAAG: SERVE HERE, A SEAT THERE.` · then, large: `SERVICE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without notice. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next few hours of your day. Where is one small job nobody will thank you for: a dish left in the sink, a bin to take out, a shared space to tidy, a message someone is waiting on? Choose one. Picture yourself doing it quietly, and walking away without mentioning it. Breathe in, and let the plan settle. Breathe out, and let go of being seen. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Sevapanthi. One on the path of seva: a community that, tradition says, follows Bhai Kanhaiya, living by its own work and serving anyone. Today's word.
Your line: service first. Today, do the small job you chose, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day one thousand three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Sevapanthis, who trace their community to Bhai Kanhaiya, are remembered for serving travelers and the sick and for living by their own work; seva in the langar and the shoe room is part of everyday Sikh life.
